body.text: How do you tell a hand-knotted silk/wool carpet from a machine-made one?

Flip the carpet over immediately. On a genuine hand-knotted Anatolian rug—typically tied with the symmetrical [Turkish/Gördes double knot](https://www.londonhouserugs.co.uk/rug-origin/turkish-rugs)—every knot is visible on the back with slight human irregularities, and the fringes are continuous extensions of the vertical warp threads rather than sewn-on strips glued to the edge.

Machine-made rugs look unnaturally uniform on the underside, often showing neat horizontal backing ridges or latex glue. For silk pieces (such as Hereke carpets), be wary of "bamboo silk," "art silk," or mercerized cotton sold at pure-silk prices; real mulberry silk feels cool at first touch, warms quickly in your palm, and smells like burnt hair—never plastic or paper—in a tiny loose-fiber burn test. The same material discipline applies to [UNESCO-listed traditional Çini ceramics](https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/traditional-craftsmanship-of-cini-making-01058) (check for hand-drawn contour lines and quartz-rich clay rather than transfer decals) and leather jackets (inspect inner seam stitching and suppleness rather than glossy showroom lighting).

body.text: Why do commission-based tour stops inflate carpet prices?

Package tours, cruise excursions, and "free" factory visits routinely build 30% to 50% hidden commissions into showroom price tags to pay tour operators, drivers, and guides. Those kickbacks subsidize artificially cheap tour prices, which is why the "cooperative" or "government-supported weaving school" stop feels theatrical and high-pressure.

Legitimate licensed guides regulated by [TUREB (Union of Turkish Tourist Guides Chambers)](https://www.tureb.org.tr/) are trained cultural specialists, yet budget agencies often pressure them to meet shopping quotas. When a showroom pours endless apple tea, rolls out twenty rugs in rapid succession, and tells you a price is valid "only today because of an export grant," walk out politely. Real workshops do not need urgency scripts, and polite refusal costs nothing.
How does international shipping and customs duty work?

Modern hand-knotted carpets, kilims, ceramics, and leather goods ship easily worldwide via DHL, FedEx, or UPS with a commercial invoice and certificate of origin, while true antiques face strict Turkish export bans under [Law No. 2863 on the Conservation of Cultural and Natural Property](https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/legislation/details/10971). Always confirm destination import duties before paying.

items: Turkish Export Rules: According to the [Ministry of Foreign Affairs customs overview](https://www.mfa.gov.tr/turkiye_ye-ait-gumruk-bilgileri.en.mfa), exporting protected cultural artifacts without state museum clearance is a serious offense. If a dealer claims a rug or ceramic is "100+ years old," insist on an official museum export clearance certificate—if they hesitate, do not buy it.

Home-Country Duties: Import taxes vary by country and material. For example, [U.S. Customs and Border Protection duty guidance](https://www.cbp.gov/travel/international-visitors/know-before-you-visit/customs-duty-information) distinguishes personal exemptions from unaccompanied mailed shipments, and tariffs depend on the exact HS classification (knotted wool vs. flat-weave vs. silk).

Safe Payment & Packing: Pay by credit card (never cash wire) so you retain chargeback protection, photograph the exact rug back and front with its serial tag before wrapping, and verify full-value transit insurance on the courier waybill.

faq.q: Is haggling expected when buying a carpet in Türkiye?
faq.a: In bazaars and independent carpet shops, polite negotiation is normal—typically 15% to 30% off an honest initial quote. Fixed-price artisan studios and museum shops do not negotiate.

faq.q: Is it cheaper to carry a carpet home in luggage or ship it?
faq.a: Small kilims and runners fit neatly in checked luggage with zero courier cost. Larger wool or silk rugs are usually safer and more convenient to ship via insured DHL or FedEx.
Almost never. Many commercial showrooms near Ephesus and Cappadocia use phrases like "state-supported" or "village cooperative" as marketing language rather than official public institutions.

faq.q: How can I tell real İznik ceramics from factory souvenirs?
faq.a: Authentic çini uses high-quartz paste, hand-traced cobalt and coral-red mineral pigments, and slight brushwork variation, whereas cheap bazaar plates use flat printed decals on porous red clay.

faq.q: Can I claim a VAT (KDV) tax refund on carpets or leather?
faq.a: Yes, if you buy from a Tax-Free registered merchant, carry the goods unused in your personal luggage, and get Turkish customs stamping at the airport before departure.

faq.q: What if a shipped carpet arrives damaged or is not the one I bought?
faq.a: Photograph the piece with its tag and dimensions at the shop, keep the itemized invoice specifying fiber content and knot origin, and pay by credit card for dispute protection.
